items.question: Explain the three pillars of observability and how they apply to an ASP.NET Core Web API.
items.answer: Metrics are numeric aggregates over time — request rate, error ratio, p95 latency, thread-pool queue depth — cheap to store and ideal for alerting. Logs are discrete structured events with context (CorrelationId, OrderId) explaining what happened on a specific request. Traces are trees of timed spans (Activity) showing where milliseconds were spent across your API, SQL, and downstream HttpClient calls. ASP.NET Core exposes all three via ILogger, System.Diagnostics.Metrics, and OpenTelemetry instrumentation. Senior teams export through OTel to Application Insights or Prometheus and correlate via shared trace/correlation id.
followUps: When would you alert on metrics vs investigate with traces?
What is the RED method for APIs?
items.sixtySeconds: Metrics for aggregates and alerts — rate errors duration. Logs for what happened with structured fields. Traces for where time went across services. OTel unifies export. Correlate with trace id or CorrelationId.

items.question: What is structured logging in .NET and why is string interpolation wrong?
items.answer: Structured logging uses ILogger message templates with named placeholders: LogInformation("Order {OrderId} created", orderId). Providers serialize OrderId as a queryable field in JSON. String interpolation ($"Order {orderId}") bakes the value into one string — Elasticsearch, Seq, and Application Insights cannot index OrderId separately. Combine with BeginScope to attach CorrelationId to every log in a request without repeating it. Pass Exception as first arg to LogError for stack traces. Tune Logging:LogLevel to suppress Microsoft.AspNetCore noise in production.
followUps: How do log scopes work across async await?
When would you choose Serilog over built-in providers?
items.sixtySeconds: Message templates not interpolation. Named fields are queryable. BeginScope adds CorrelationId context. LogError takes exception first. Tune log levels per namespace. Export via App Insights or OTel.

items.question: How does distributed tracing work across microservices with OpenTelemetry in .NET?
items.answer: ASP.NET Core instrumentation creates a root span per incoming HTTP request with a trace id. When your service calls another via HttpClient, AddHttpClientInstrumentation injects the W3C traceparent header (trace-id + parent-span-id). The downstream service reads traceparent and creates a child span linked to the same trace id. Database calls add grandchild spans via EF instrumentation. Exporters send completed spans to OTLP collector, Jaeger, or Application Insights. If traceparent is missing on one hop, the distributed trace breaks — always verify HttpClient instrumentation. Custom business steps use ActivitySource.StartActivity with tags.
followUps: What is the difference between traceparent and X-Correlation-Id?
How do you handle trace sampling at 10,000 RPS?
items.sixtySeconds: Root span per request. HttpClient injects traceparent. Child spans share trace id. OTLP export. Custom ActivitySource for business logic. Filter health checks. Ratio sampling for cost. Broken propagation = orphan spans.

items.question: Diagnose a production API that is slow under load using dotnet-counters — what do you look for?
items.answer: Run dotnet-counters monitor against the process with System.Runtime and Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting counters. threadpool-queue-length sustained above zero indicates thread-pool starvation — often sync-over-async (.Result, .Wait()) or blocking I/O on async endpoints. Rising gen-2-gc-count and gc-heap-size suggest allocation pressure or large object heap issues. Compare requests-per-second to current-requests for queue buildup. If CPU is high but queue is zero, capture dotnet-trace cpu-sampling profile to find hot methods. Cross-check Application Insights dependency duration to separate in-process starvation from slow SQL.
followUps: What is the difference between dotnet-counters and dotnet-trace?
How does thread-pool starvation relate to sync-over-async?
items.sixtySeconds: dotnet-counters monitor live. Watch threadpool-queue-length for starvation. gen-2-gc-count for allocation issues. If CPU high use dotnet-trace. Join with App Insights dependency times to rule out database.

items.question: Design Kubernetes health probes for an ASP.NET Core API with database dependency and slow startup.
items.answer: Register AddHealthChecks with tags: 'live' for a trivial self-check only (process responds), 'ready' for NpgSql/Redis dependency checks with 2-second timeout. Map /health/live with Predicate live tags and /health/ready with ready tags returning 503 when Unhealthy. Configure K8s livenessProbe on /health/live (period 15s), readinessProbe on /health/ready (period 10s), startupProbe on /health/ready with failureThreshold 30 and periodSeconds 5 for up to 150s EF migration warm-up. Exclude probes from JWT auth and OTel trace sampling. Never put database on liveness — DB blip should remove pod from load balancer (readiness), not restart it.
followUps: What happens if all pods fail readiness during a database outage?
Should Degraded status return 200 or 503 on readiness?
items.sixtySeconds: Tagged checks. Live self only — restart on fail. Ready includes DB — remove from LB on fail. startupProbe for migrations. Separate endpoints. Unauthenticated. Never DB on liveness.

items.question: Implement correlation ID propagation from API gateway through HttpClient to a downstream service.
items.answer: Early middleware reads X-Correlation-Id header or generates GUID (or uses Activity.TraceId). Store in HttpContext.Items, add to response header via OnStarting, wrap pipeline in logger.BeginScope with CorrelationId. Register CorrelationIdHandler as DelegatingHandler on typed HttpClient — copies header to outbound requests. OpenTelemetry HttpClient instrumentation adds traceparent separately. On errors, Problem Details CustomizeProblemDetails adds correlationId extension. For message queues, embed CorrelationId in event payload or application properties. Support staff searches one id across all services in Application Insights.
followUps: Should each microservice generate a new correlation id?
How do background workers inherit correlation from HTTP?
items.sixtySeconds: Middleware read or create id. BeginScope for logs. DelegatingHandler on HttpClient. Return in response and Problem Details. traceparent for spans. Queue message headers for async.

items.question: How do you debug a slow endpoint in Application Insights production?
items.answer: Open Failures or Performance blade, find the slow operation or filter requests by duration > 2s. Open end-to-end transaction view for a sample — waterfall shows child Dependency telemetry (SQL, HTTP) with individual durations. Note operation_Id. Run KQL: join requests to dependencies on operation_Id to aggregate which dependency name has highest p95. Check if slowness is external (dependency) or in-process (gap between spans). Correlate with custom CorrelationId property if support provided it. Verify deploy timestamp and dependency failure rate on Application Map.
followUps: What is operation_Id vs trace id?
How does adaptive sampling affect your investigation?
items.sixtySeconds: Transaction view waterfall. operation_Id links request and dependencies. KQL join for p95 by dependency name. Application Map for topology. Check if SQL or HttpClient is the bottleneck.

items.question: Liveness vs readiness — a candidate puts PostgreSQL check on /health used for both probes. What goes wrong?
items.answer: When PostgreSQL has a transient network blip, liveness probe fails because the shared endpoint returns 503. Kubernetes restarts the pod. All replicas restart simultaneously during a shared DB issue, causing a restart storm instead of graceful traffic drain. Correct design: liveness /health/live checks only that the process responds (tags live). Readiness /health/ready includes PostgreSQL (tags ready) — failure removes pod from Service endpoints without restart. Pod recovers automatically when DB returns. This is a common FAANG-style scenario question testing understanding of K8s failure actions.
followUps: When would you use a startupProbe?
How do you prevent health checks from polluting traces?
items.sixtySeconds: DB on liveness means DB blip restarts all pods. Readiness removes from LB without restart. Liveness is dumb self-check. Separate endpoints with tags. startupProbe for slow boot.

items.question: What metrics would you alert on for a public Web API and which tools collect them?
items.answer: Alert on: HTTP 5xx error rate > 1% over 5 minutes, p95 request duration > SLO threshold (e.g. 500ms), dependency failure rate spike, and optionally threadpool-queue-length via custom export. ASP.NET Core publishes http.server.request.duration histogram via OpenTelemetry. AddPrometheusExporter with Grafana alert rules, or Application Insights smart detection and metric alerts. Use RED: Rate (requests/s), Errors (5xx ratio), Duration (p95). Avoid alerting on averages. Complement with synthetic availability tests hitting /health/ready from multiple regions.
followUps: Why is high-cardinality UserId label dangerous on Prometheus counters?
What is the USE method for infrastructure?
items.sixtySeconds: Alert 5xx rate and p95 latency. RED method. OTel metrics to Prometheus or App Insights. Not averages — p95. dotnet-counters for live thread pool during incidents. Synthetic probes for uptime.

items.question: Compare OpenTelemetry export to Application Insights vs self-hosted Prometheus for a microservice fleet.
items.answer: Application Insights (UseAzureMonitor): fastest Azure setup, built-in transaction view, Application Map, smart detection, KQL — good when already on Azure; cost scales with ingestion volume; adaptive sampling required at high QPS. Prometheus + Grafana: OSS, Kubernetes-native scraping, long-retention custom dashboards, no per-telemetry ingestion pricing — but you operate storage, alerting, and trace backend (Tempo/Jaeger) separately. OTel Collector as hub exports to both — vendor-neutral instrumentation in each .NET service, fan-out to App Insights for ops team and Prometheus for SRE dashboards. Senior answer: instrument once with OTel, choose backends per team needs.
followUps: How do you migrate from legacy ApplicationInsights SDK to OTel?
What is tail-based sampling?
items.sixtySeconds: OTel instrument once. App Insights fast on Azure transaction view sampling cost. Prometheus OSS K8s native self-operate. Collector fan-out to both. Unique cloud_RoleName per microservice.
